newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Laws picks Peters for NZ finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Laws picks Peters for NZ finance minister.

text.p: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters should be finance minister in the new coalition government, his former strategist said on Friday.
Former MP and NZ First strategist Michael Laws said in his regular column in Wellington's Evening Post newspaper that Peters needed the portfolio for political reasons.
"He needs a top prize and...despite the horror stories of the financial markets, he is no extremist and takes good advice," Laws said.

NZ First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and is negotiating separately with the conservative caretaker National Party government and the main opposition Labour Party over the shape of the next government.
Laws, a long time friend of Peters, also attacked "subjective, self-interested and speculative" economic commentators.
"Reserve Bank governor Don Brash is clearly their patron.

"His injudicious attempt to influence coalition talks this week by speculating that increased government investment in the crisis areas of child health, law and order, and education would be inflationary -- and hence wrong -- received coverage well beyond its worth," Laws said.
On Monday Brash said planned tax cuts may have to be deferred if net spending increased.
Peters is seen as a near certainty for deputy prime minister.
But Laws said as leader of the junior coalition partner, Peters would have to be given one of the three key roles of prime minister, foreign affairs minister or finance minister.
The leader of the larger coalition partner would automatically assume the prime minister's role, and Peters offered the foreign affairs role to Labour's Mike Moore during the election campaign.
That left only finance, Laws said.
He said Peters needed to consider how he was positioning himself for the next election.
"Winston must build a reputation for solidity as well as creativity.
"He must be in a position to deliver to his beloved export community. He must be able to make a visible mark in Parliament over the next three years.
"In addition, he must stay at home."
Laws said neither alternative finance minister -- Bill Birch or Michael Cullen -- was indispensable.
Cullen was "no natural" at the portfolio and had "a profligate nature" if Labour's election manifesto was any indication.
Cullen also did not deserve Labour leader Helen Clark's loyalty after having conspired against her earlier this year.
Three-quarters of National's caucus were "itching" for reasons to dump Birch.
Laws said after Peters assumed the role of finance spokesman for NZ First midway through this year the party's economic policies had become more moderate.
Most commentators have credited Laws with moving NZ First's policies towards National.

Modest spending proposals, a commitment to low inflation, more rational housing and tertiary education policies and a softening of the party's foreign investment policy had all occurred only after Peters had dropped Nelson schoolteacher Bernard Downey as finance spokesman and assumed the role himself. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
